newsitem.title: GERMANY: Courier group criticises Deutsche Post pricing.
newsitem.headline: Courier group criticises Deutsche Post pricing.

text.p: The German post office and a group of shipping companies seeking a liberalised market in Germany on Monday lashed out at each other in an increasingly bitter dispute over parcel delivery pricing.

The Federation of International Express and Courier Services (BIEK) said it expected the European Commission to take action against Deutsche Post AG for allegedly covering up more than two billion marks in parcel post losses each year.
But Deutsche Post said parcel losses totaled only 1.5 billion marks in 1996, and were expected to fall to one billion marks in 1997.
They do not have the right figures," Deutsche Post spokesman Martin Dobychai told Reuters.

BIEK, which includes the German units of DHL Worldwide Express, Federal Express, TNT Express and United Parcel Service, filed a complaint to the European Commission, which last month reached a preliminary finding that Deutsche Post employed anti-competitive practices in parcel delivery.
The German postal monopoly used "unnecessarily high" rates for letters to subsidise parcel prices that illegally hinder competition, the Commission said in a letter to Deutsche Post.
The Commission expected to hear a response from Deutsche Post this spring before reaching a final decision by fall.
BIEK in a news conference said a German Cartel Office inquiry into Deutsche Post's pricing found the post office had piled up more than 10 billion marks in parcel deficits from 1992 to 1996.
"We think this subsidising will be stopped by Brussels," said Ralf Wojtek, an attorney for BIEK.

He also said the parcel losses could handicap Deutsche Post's plan to float shares on the stock market by the year 2000. "We see no possibility of reducing these deficits in the foreseeable future," Wojtek said. "It would be impossible to enter the market with losses like that."
BIEK said it wanted Deutsche Post broken up into a competitive parcel service and a separate unit with a monopoly on letter delivery. BIEK's other five members are German courier enterprises.

The German government last week outlined a bill that would preserve Deutsche Post's monopoly until 2003 on letters weighing less than 100 grams. Delivery of heavier parcels would be open to full competition on January 1, 1998.
Deutsche Post had no plans to break up its business, Dobychai said.

He also dismissed a delay in any share offering because of the package deficits. "The losses are getting smaller every year and by the year 2000 we expect the freight business to be on the positive side," he said.
Deutsche Post, which had 1996 revenue of 15.5 billion marks, last month signed a union contract expected to cut freight costs by 700 million marks, he added.
